subject: biology
title: Biomolecules
subtitle: Metabolites, the structure of proteins, carbohydrates and nucleic acids, and the nature and action of enzymes

seo.meta_description: NEET Biology — Biomolecules: primary & secondary metabolites, amino acids, lipids and sugars, the four levels of protein structure, polysaccharides, nucleic acids and DNA base pairing, and enzymes (mechanism, factors, six classes, cofactors), with NEET-level examples and MCQs. Free on Vidaara.

summary:
• Metabolites: primary (amino acids, sugars, nucleotides — direct roles) and secondary (alkaloids, rubber, pigments, antibiotics — ecological/human use).
  • Building blocks & bonds: amino acids → proteins (peptide bonds); monosaccharides → polysaccharides (glycosidic bonds); nucleotides → nucleic acids (phosphodiester bonds); lipids (MW < 800, not true macromolecules).
  • Protein structure: primary (sequence) → secondary (helix/sheet) → tertiary (3D) → quaternary (e.g. haemoglobin, 4 subunits). Collagen is the most abundant animal protein.
  • Polysaccharides: starch (helical, stores; blue with iodine), glycogen (animal store), cellulose (structural, no helix).
  • Nucleic acids: purines (A, G) & pyrimidines (C, T/U); DNA double helix — A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds), antiparallel.
  • Enzymes: protein biocatalysts; lower activation energy; affected by temperature, pH, substrate; 6 classes; holoenzyme = apoenzyme + cofactor.

faqs.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary metabolites?
faqs.a: Primary metabolites such as amino acids, sugars and nucleotides have identifiable, direct roles in normal physiological processes. Secondary metabolites — alkaloids, flavonoids, rubber, essential oils, antibiotics and pigments — have no direct role in basic metabolism but are useful ecologically and to humans.

faqs.q: Name the four levels of protein structure with one feature each.
faqs.a: Primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids; secondary structure is local folding into an alpha-helix or beta-pleated sheet; tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of the chain; and quaternary structure is the assembly of two or more polypeptide chains, as in haemoglobin's four subunits.

faqs.q: Which bonds join the monomers in proteins, polysaccharides and nucleic acids?
faqs.a: Amino acids in proteins are joined by peptide bonds; monosaccharides in polysaccharides by glycosidic bonds; and nucleotides in nucleic acids by phosphodiester bonds.

faqs.q: What is a holoenzyme, an apoenzyme and a cofactor?
faqs.a: Many enzymes need a non-protein helper called a cofactor. The complete, catalytically active enzyme (protein + cofactor) is the holoenzyme; its protein part alone is the apoenzyme. Cofactors include metal ions, prosthetic groups and organic coenzymes (often derived from vitamins).

faqs.q: How does competitive inhibition work? Give the classic example.
faqs.a: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and binds the enzyme's active site, competing with the substrate and lowering the reaction rate; it can be overcome by raising substrate concentration. The classic example is malonate, which competitively inhibits succinic dehydrogenase (whose substrate is succinate).

topics.title: Chemical Analysis, Metabolites and the Building Blocks
topics.concept:
If we grind any living tissue, make an extract and analyse it chemically, we find two kinds of compounds. The acid-soluble pool contains small molecules of low molecular weight — amino acids, monosaccharides (sugars), nucleotides and lipids — while the acid-insoluble fraction contains the giant macromolecules: proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides. A frequently tested subtlety is that lipids, although they appear in the acid-insoluble fraction, have molecular weights under about 800 and are therefore not true macromolecules; they sediment there only because they form parts of membranes.

The thousands of small organic compounds in a cell are called metabolites, and NCERT divides them into two groups. Primary metabolites — amino acids, sugars, nucleotides, fatty acids — have clear, identifiable roles in normal physiology (growth, energy, structure). Secondary metabolites — alkaloids (morphine, codeine), flavonoids, rubber, essential oils, antibiotics, coloured pigments (carotenoids, anthocyanins), gums and spices — have no obvious role in basic metabolism but are of great ecological and human importance. Recognising examples of each category is a guaranteed NEET mark.

The building blocks themselves are worth knowing. Amino acids are organic acids that carry an amino group (–NH₂), a carboxyl group (–COOH) and a variable side chain (R) on the same carbon; twenty of them build all proteins, and at cellular pH they exist as dipolar zwitterions. Lipids are usually water-insoluble and include fats and oils (glycerol esterified with fatty acids) and phospholipids; fatty acids may be saturated (no double bonds) or unsaturated (with double bonds).

Carbohydrates (sugars) range from simple monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, the pentose ribose) through oligosaccharides to long polysaccharides. The most abundant biomolecule in the whole living world is in fact a polysaccharide — cellulose. These four classes of building blocks — amino acids, sugars, nucleotides and fatty acids — are the monomers from which the cell assembles its macromolecules, the subject of the next topic.

examples.problem: Classify each as a primary or secondary metabolite: glucose, morphine, an amino acid, rubber.
examples.solution: Glucose and the amino acid are primary metabolites (direct physiological roles). Morphine (an alkaloid) and rubber are secondary metabolites.

examples.problem: Why are lipids found in the acid-insoluble fraction although they are not macromolecules?
examples.solution: Their molecular weight is under ~800, so chemically they are not macromolecules; they appear in the acid-insoluble fraction only because they are organised into membranes that sediment together as cellular fragments.

quiz.q: Which of these is a secondary metabolite?
quiz.explanation: Morphine is an alkaloid — a secondary metabolite.

quiz.q: Lipids are generally NOT classed as macromolecules because their molecular weight is:
quiz.explanation: Lipid MW is under ~800, below the macromolecule range.

quiz.q: An amino acid contains which two functional groups on the same carbon?
quiz.explanation: Amino acids bear an amino (–NH₂) and a carboxyl (–COOH) group.

quiz.q: The most abundant biomolecule in the living world is:
quiz.explanation: Cellulose (a polysaccharide) is the most abundant biomolecule.

quiz.q: At cellular pH, an amino acid exists mainly as a:
quiz.explanation: Amino acids are dipolar zwitterions at cellular pH.

topics.note: NEET tip: Sort metabolites fast — primary = amino acids/sugars/nucleotides; secondary = alkaloids/rubber/antibiotics/pigments. Remember lipids are NOT macromolecules, and cellulose is the most abundant biomolecule.

topics.title: Proteins and Polysaccharides
topics.concept:
Proteins are the most abundant biomacromolecules and are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Their roles are vast: they act as enzymes, as transporters (the glucose transporter GLUT-4), as antibodies, as some hormones and receptors, and as structural materials. The most abundant protein in the whole animal world is collagen, while the most abundant protein in the entire biosphere is the photosynthetic enzyme RuBisCO.

A protein's shape is described at four levels, a classic NEET topic. The primary structure is simply the linear sequence of amino acids, with a defined N-terminal and C-terminal end. The secondary structure is the regular local folding of that chain into shapes such as the right-handed alpha-helix or the beta-pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds. The tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of the whole chain into a compact shape, essential for biological activity.

The highest level, the quaternary structure, arises only when a functional protein is built from two or more polypeptide chains (subunits) assembled together — the textbook example is haemoglobin, made of four subunits (two alpha and two beta). Not every protein has a quaternary structure, but identifying haemoglobin as the standard example, and matching each level to its description, is reliably examined.

Polysaccharides are long chains of monosaccharides linked by glycosidic bonds, and three are key. Starch is the storage carbohydrate of plants: it is a helically coiled molecule (amylose plus branched amylopectin) and forms a blue-black colour with iodine because iodine slots into its helix. Glycogen is the more highly branched storage carbohydrate of animals. Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide of plant cell walls; it has no helix and no iodine colour because it is made of straight chains of β-glucose. Chitin (in fungal walls and arthropod exoskeletons) is a nitrogen-containing structural polysaccharide. Remembering 'starch = helix + iodine-blue, cellulose = straight + structural, glycogen = animal store' covers the common questions.

examples.problem: Haemoglobin is made of four polypeptide chains. Which level of protein structure does this represent?
examples.solution: The assembly of multiple polypeptide chains into one functional molecule is the quaternary structure — haemoglobin's four subunits are the classic example.

examples.problem: Why does starch give a blue colour with iodine while cellulose does not?
examples.solution: Starch is helically coiled, and iodine fits inside the helix to give the blue-black colour. Cellulose consists of straight, unbranched chains with no helix, so iodine cannot lodge in it and no colour develops.

quiz.q: Amino acids in a protein are joined by:
quiz.explanation: Peptide bonds link amino acids.

quiz.q: The most abundant protein in the animal world is:
quiz.explanation: Collagen is the most abundant animal protein.

quiz.q: Quaternary structure is best illustrated by:
quiz.explanation: Haemoglobin (4 subunits) shows quaternary structure.

quiz.q: The storage polysaccharide of animals is:
quiz.explanation: Glycogen is the animal storage polysaccharide.

quiz.q: Cellulose differs from starch in that it:
options: has no helix and is structural
quiz.explanation: Cellulose is straight-chained and structural; it gives no iodine colour.

topics.note: NEET tip: Protein levels: primary (sequence) → secondary (helix/sheet) → tertiary (3D) → quaternary (haemoglobin = 4). Polysaccharides: starch (helix, iodine-blue), glycogen (animal), cellulose (structural, no helix).

topics.title: Nucleic Acids and the Bonds in Biomolecules
topics.concept:
Nucleic acids — DNA and RNA — are the macromolecules that store and transmit genetic information. They are polymers of nucleotides, and each nucleotide has three parts: a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA) and a phosphate group. A base joined only to the sugar (no phosphate) is a nucleoside. The nucleotides are linked into a chain by phosphodiester bonds between the phosphate of one and the sugar of the next.

The nitrogenous bases fall into two groups, a guaranteed NEET fact: the double-ringed purines are adenine (A) and guanine (G), and the single-ringed pyrimidines are cytosine (C), thymine (T) (found in DNA) and uracil (U) (which replaces thymine in RNA). So DNA uses A, G, C, T while RNA uses A, G, C, U.

The Watson–Crick double helix of DNA has two strands that run antiparallel (one 5'→3', the other 3'→5') and are coiled into a right-handed helix. The strands are held together by complementary base pairing: adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds (A=T) and guanine pairs with cytosine through three hydrogen bonds (G≡C). This is why Chargaff's rule holds — the amount of A equals T and G equals C. The B-form helix makes one full turn every 10 base pairs (pitch 3.4 nm, with 0.34 nm between adjacent base pairs).

It helps to collect the bonds of biomolecules in one place, because NEET often asks which bond joins which monomer. Peptide bonds link amino acids in proteins; glycosidic bonds link sugars in polysaccharides; phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides in nucleic acids; and weaker hydrogen bonds stabilise the secondary and higher structures of proteins and hold the two strands of DNA together. Mastering this short list resolves a whole family of questions.

examples.problem: If one DNA strand has the sequence 5'-ATGC-3', what is the sequence of the complementary strand?
examples.solution: Pairing A with T and G with C and keeping the strands antiparallel, the complement is 3'-TACG-5' (i.e. written 5'→3' it is 5'-GCAT-3').

examples.problem: Which base pair is held by three hydrogen bonds, and why does that matter?
examples.solution: The guanine≡cytosine (G≡C) pair has three hydrogen bonds (A=T has only two). More G≡C pairs therefore make a DNA molecule more thermally stable (harder to denature).

quiz.q: The purine bases are:
quiz.explanation: Adenine and guanine are the double-ringed purines.

quiz.q: In RNA, thymine is replaced by:
quiz.explanation: RNA uses uracil instead of thymine.

quiz.q: The G≡C base pair is held by:
quiz.explanation: G pairs with C via three hydrogen bonds.

quiz.q: Nucleotides in a nucleic acid are joined by:
quiz.explanation: Phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides.

quiz.q: In B-form DNA, the number of base pairs per complete turn is about:
quiz.explanation: B-DNA has ~10 base pairs per turn.

topics.note: NEET tip: Purines (A, G) double-ring; pyrimidines (C, T, U) single-ring. A=T (2 bonds), G≡C (3 bonds), antiparallel, 10 bp/turn. Bonds: peptide (protein), glycosidic (sugar), phosphodiester (nucleic acid).

topics.title: Enzymes
topics.concept:
Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up the chemical reactions of life; almost all are proteins (a few RNA molecules, called ribozymes, are catalytic too). An enzyme works by lowering the activation energy needed for a reaction, so the reaction proceeds far faster without the enzyme itself being consumed. The reactant binds to a specific pocket on the enzyme called the active site, forming a transient enzyme–substrate complex that passes through an unstable transition state before products are released.

Because enzymes are proteins, their activity is sensitive to conditions, and NEET expects the standard graphs. Each enzyme has an optimum temperature and an optimum pH; above the optimum, high temperature or extreme pH denatures the protein and activity falls sharply. As substrate concentration rises, the rate increases and then plateaus at a maximum velocity (Vmax) when all active sites are saturated. Some molecules slow enzymes by inhibition: in competitive inhibition, an inhibitor that resembles the substrate competes for the active site — the classic example is malonate, which competitively inhibits succinic dehydrogenase (whose true substrate is succinate).

Enzymes are grouped by the type of reaction they catalyse into six classes, which you should be able to list: oxidoreductases (oxidation–reduction), transferases (transfer of a group), hydrolases (hydrolysis), lyases (removal of groups forming double bonds, not by hydrolysis), isomerases (interconversion of isomers) and ligases (joining two molecules using ATP). A simple way to remember them is the order OTHLIL: Oxidoreductase, Transferase, Hydrolase, Lyase, Isomerase, Ligase.

Many enzymes are active only when a non-protein helper, a cofactor, is attached. The protein part on its own is the apoenzyme, and the complete, catalytically active enzyme (apoenzyme + cofactor) is the holoenzyme. Cofactors are of three kinds: tightly bound prosthetic groups (e.g. haem in peroxidase), loosely bound organic coenzymes (often derived from vitamins, such as NAD and NADP from niacin), and metal ions (e.g. zinc in carbonic anhydrase). The relations 'holoenzyme = apoenzyme + cofactor' and the malonate–succinate example are among the most frequently asked enzyme facts.

examples.problem: Malonate slows the action of succinic dehydrogenase, and adding more succinate restores the rate. What type of inhibition is this?
examples.solution: Competitive inhibition — malonate resembles the substrate succinate and competes for the active site, so increasing the substrate concentration outcompetes it and restores the rate.
The apoenzyme is the protein part of an enzyme alone (inactive). The holoenzyme is the complete, active enzyme — apoenzyme plus its cofactor.

quiz.q: Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering the:
quiz.explanation: Enzymes lower the activation energy of a reaction.

quiz.q: Malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase by:
quiz.explanation: Malonate competes with succinate for the active site.

quiz.q: Enzymes that join two molecules using ATP are:
quiz.explanation: Ligases join molecules using ATP.

quiz.q: The complete, catalytically active enzyme is the:
quiz.explanation: Holoenzyme = apoenzyme + cofactor.

quiz.q: Coenzymes are often derived from:
quiz.explanation: Many coenzymes (e.g. NAD/NADP) are derived from vitamins.

topics.note: NEET tip: Remember the six classes (OTHLIL), the malonate–succinate competitive-inhibition example, and 'holoenzyme = apoenzyme + cofactor' (cofactors = prosthetic group / coenzyme / metal ion).

R: Malonate is a competitive inhibitor that competes with succinate for the active site.
options: Both A and R true, R explains A

questions.explanation: Because the inhibition is competitive, excess substrate outcompetes the inhibitor — R explains A.
